title: Prefix bucketing + inline quantization / KV hotswap — Lynx Tech technical review
summary: Deep technical session on enabling 128k+ context with a focus on prefix bucketing, inline quantization tradeoffs, and a plan for safe KV hotswap in a VPC/on-prem deployment. Covered expected latency/throughput, batching windows, fallback routes, and initial bench numbers to run on Lynx's infra.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~82 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording link: (redacted)

Attendees:
- Jordan Miles (Redwood, AE)
- Eleni Park (Redwood, SE)
- Rahul Desai (Redwood, Infra PM)
- Ava Chen (Lynx Tech, CTO)
- Mateo Ruiz (Lynx Tech, Head of ML)
- Samir Patel (Lynx Tech, Infra Eng)
- Nina Osei (Lynx Tech, Security)

---

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about an hour twenty. This is the technical deep dive to go over Lynx's long-context plan — prefix bucketing, inline quantization, and that KV hotswap idea you mentioned. Eleni and Rahul from our infra folks are here.

[00:18] Ava: Yep thanks, quick context: we're running a document ingestion pipeline with lots of long legal docs, want persistent 128k+ context for multimodal retrieval + generation. High QPS during business hours but strict 200ms p95 generation SLO for short-turn queries; longer batched jobs can be higher. We're evaluating hosted vs Private in our VPC.

[00:35] Eleni: Cool, can you tell us current stack? Mateo, Samir, quick?

[00:44] Mateo: We're on K8s on-prem for sensitive workloads, GCP for burst. Models currently 70B FP16, nightly compaction to 32-bit quant for storage, using a home-grown KV store for doc embeddings. Latency for a 4k prefix is ~120ms p50 on our nodes, but it balloons at 64k.

[01:03] Samir: Also note, we have strict no-exfil policy, so any data plane move must be VPC-only, HSM for keys.

[01:12] Jordan: Understood. Today we'll run through three patterns that help: 1) prefix bucketing to reduce active attention window, 2) inline quantization strategies (mixed precision vs per-layer fine-grain), and 3) a KV hotswap pattern so you can move between memory tiers without losing in-flight requests. We'll talk micro-latency numbers and what to bench.

[01:45] Eleni: Quick note on terminology — when I say "bucketing" I'm referring to grouping recent prefixes into a small active KV set and shadowing older prefixes into a cold tier. This reduces sequence length for the attention kernel. We'll sketch the eviction and fetch costs.

[02:10] Mateo: Sounds good. Does this mean we drop context fidelity? We need accurate citations in the last 512 tokens at least.

[02:23] Eleni: Good point. Bucketing is priority-based: recent prefixes kept intact, older prefixes kept as compressed summaries (we call them "anchors") so you retain citation links. We discussed lossy vs lossless approaches.

[03:01] (roughly 3m mark) Jordan: Let's go through a live sketch — assume a 200k input split into 8k windows. We'll do an append/lookup pipeline: recent N windows live in GPU memory (fast KV), older windows compressed on NVMe with quantized keys.

[03:28] [03:28] Samir: How many windows do you typically keep hot?

[03:32] Eleni: Depends on traffic. In our ops we've seen 3-6 hot buckets per shard keeps average seq length to under 32k for most queries. That buys you throughput without sacrificing last-n token fidelity.

[03:51] Ava: Can you be more concrete about latency? Our SLO is 200ms p95 for short queries, but many queries will touch historical context.

[04:00] Rahul: Right, we target two latency classes: fast path (<=200ms) that only touches hot buckets and cached prefixes; slow path (<=1.2s) for warm fetch from NVMe and inline quant decode. We bias routing so that if hot miss and query is latency-sensitive we'll fallback to a smaller compressed summary response rather than full decode.

[04:36] [04:36] Mateo: What are the costs of inline quantization decompress on the slow path?

[04:41] Eleni: Compression formats matter. Inline 8-bit quant with a fast dequant kernel costs ~40-70ms on an A100 for a 64k window decode; 4-bit asymmetric may cost a bit more on decode if we're doing DP per-tensor scales. The trick is to do partial dequant: only dequantize KV entries that the attention actually touches. That's where sparse attention helps.

[05:12] Jordan: I'll toss an example: workload X at 128k full context, when using prefix bucketing + partial inline dequant, we saw tail latencies drop from ~2.3s to ~950ms on our internal bench with similar model sizes. Not identical to your infra, but indicative.

[05:43] Samir: Partial dequant sounds promising but is it safe for on-prem with HSM? We need keys to never leave the VPC.

[05:54] Rahul: Yes. The data plane always stays in your VPC in our Private deployment; dequant ops and KV tiers run on your nodes. Redwood's control plane only manages images and config. We'll show deployment diagrams.

[06:20] [06:20] (Eleni screenshare: architecture diagram)

[06:35] Eleni: Here we have three tiers: GPU memory (hot KV), NVMe local (warm), and network-backed cold store (object). Hotswap is a coordinated state-transfer: when we promote a bucket from warm to hot we insert a new KV root pointer and atomically switch the routing table while draining in-flight requests against the old pointer.

[07:04] Ava: Atomic switch — how do you guarantee in-flight KV consistency? What if an in-flight request references an address that moves mid-request?

[07:14] Eleni: We run per-request pinning. Once a request starts, it pins a KV root version; promotions create new versions but we keep last N versions readable until pinned requests finish. We garbage collect after grace window. This prevents torn reads.

[07:42] Mateo: That pinning also increases memory retention — how big is N typically?

[07:47] Eleni: N=2-4 in production, depends on median request length and streaming window. We keep small N to avoid memory blowout.

[08:05] [08:05] Jordan: Let's switch to batching: you mentioned throughput peaks. What batch sizes and batching windows are you comfortable with?

[08:14] Samir: For user-facing latency we want batching under 8ms if we can, otherwise we expose latency. Background indexing can be larger.

[08:22] Eleni: Redwood's continuous batching has a configurable max wait (we often use 3-8ms for low-latency paths) and a dynamic max batch size based on token count. For long-context requests batching by prefix length helps: group similar-length requests to reduce wasted compute and KV fetch divergence.

[08:48] Mateo: Grouping by length... do you mean bucketing by token-length in the router?

[08:53] Eleni: Yes, the router classifies request shape and routes to compatible serving instances. We also have a small fast-path worker pool for <=4k requests.

[09:12] [09:12] Nina: Security question — for Private in VPC, what about audit logs and KMS integration?

[09:18] Rahul: Supports customer-managed KMS, HSMs, and audit log ingestion to your SIEM. Everything in the data plane is logged locally; Redwood's control plane logs only operational events.

[09:33] Nina: Good. We need SOC2 and local retention controls.

[09:40] Jordan: We'll send the compliance packet after the call; we'll also include architecture diagrams for audit.

[09:51] [09:51] (15m summary pause)

[10:05] Jordan: Back to inline quant: Mate0, sorry Mateo, earlier you said you compact to 32-bit nightly — if we move to 4-bit or 2-bit storage for cold tiers we can save NVMe bandwidth, but quality regressions depend on per-layer sensitivity. We recommend per-layer calibration and a small fixed FP16 shadow for critical heads.

[10:35] Mateo: Can we run AB tests to measure hallucination/regression?

[10:40] Eleni: Absolutely — Redwood Optimize integrates eval hooks. You push a test set and we run quality diffs on the rollouts. For inline quant we typically do a canary on 5% of traffic, measure BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics and hallucination signals tied to prompt sets.

[11:02] (brief cross-talk, note: transcription sometimes shows 'Mate0' mistaken for name)

[11:20] Jordan: Let's do an example bench plan for you to run on your infra: 1) baseline p95/p99 for 4k, 32k, 128k full decode, 2) prefix-bucketing with 3 hot buckets, partial dequant only for attended KV, 3) inline 8-bit and 4-bit variants with per-layer calibration, 4) simulate 10% canary with KV hotswap promotions at 60s intervals.

[11:54] Samir: For bench infra, we'll need a script or harness.

[11:57] Jordan: We'll share our perf harness (link in notes). It runs microbench for attention kernel, KV fetch latencies, and end-to-end generation with streaming.

[12:08] Eleni: Also watch out for GC pauses on the NVMe tier — certain OS configs readahead can cause jitter. Tune I/O scheduler and use fio to verify.

[12:22] Ava: What about fallback when NVMe fails or is slow? We need graceful degradation that doesn't leak secrets or show partial hallucinations.

[12:32] Rahul: Two layers: safe fallback that returns a compressed summary instead of full context, and a protective guardrail in the decoder that flags low-confidence tokens. You can configure to fail closed (reject) or fail open (summary) depending on compliance.

[12:58] [12:58] (30-minute mark)

[13:08] Mateo: Tell us more about the hotswap state machine.

[13:12] Eleni: It's a four-phase protocol: 1) prepare: stream and pre-validate new bucket into warm tier; 2) promote: atomically update route table to new KV root; 3) drain: let pinned requests finish on old root; 4) commit/GC: move final pointers and garbage collect. Each step has timeouts and rollback options.

[13:42] Samir: How does this affect latency for concurrent reads?

[13:48] Eleni: Minimal — the route switch is O(1) pointer swap. Draining keeps the old root live so requests already started are unaffected. The main impact is temporary increased memory footprint while both roots are present.

[14:05] Jordan: We recommend a canary promotion window during low traffic; automatic rollback if error rates spike beyond threshold.

[14:17] Ava: Can Redwood's console show these promotions and GC metrics?

[14:22] Rahul: Yes, per-route metrics, timeline of promotions, memory usage, and pinned-request counts. We'll grant you a demo tenant.

[14:35] [14:35] (Eleni drops an implementation note)

[14:40] Eleni: Also, for partial dequant we use a heatmap of attention weights to select keys to dequant; that selection itself is cheap — a sparse lookup on top-k keys by approximate locality-sensitive hashing so it's sub-ms typically.

[15:02] Mateo: LSH adds complexity, can we approximate with simple frequency heuristics?

[15:09] Eleni: Yes, frequency heuristics (recentness + token overlap) are simpler to implement, but LSH gives better precision for long docs. Tradeoff depends on your throughput needs.

[15:28] Samir: On quantization — do you recommend symmetric or asymmetric quant?

[15:33] Eleni: For KV keys, asymmetric 4-bit with per-block scales often performs best. For activations we use per-channel scales and sometimes grouped quant. The decoder logits are left in FP16.

[15:50] [15:50] Jordan: Let's talk numbers: in our internal tests on A100 nodes with 4-bit inline and prefix bucketing, throughput improved ~1.8x and token-cost dropped ~40% for 128k workloads compared to naive full-decoding. But p99 still depends on NVMe fetch jitter.

[16:11] Ava: We'll want to see the raw bench results — can you share the CSV?

[16:16] Jordan: Yes, we'll attach the bench artifacts and the harness.

[16:25] [16:25] (QA starts)

[16:27] Nina: Compliance — do you store KV metadata outside of VPC for routing?

[16:33] Rahul: No customer metadata is stored outside unless you opt into Redwood-managed discovery. For Private we keep the routing table locally; control plane only stores opaque identifiers.

[16:50] Mateo: We have a question about multi-tenant vs single-tenant: is it safe to co-locate buckets from different customers on same GPU?

[16:58] Eleni: Co-location is doable with strong tenant isolation; we recommend dedicated capacity for high-sensitivity customers. Co-locating is usually fine for cost reasons but requires strict RBAC and mem isolation.

[17:18] Samir: If we go private on-prem, what changes? Do we still get Redwood's Optimize recommendations?

[17:23] Jordan: Yes, Optimize can run in air-gapped mode with the evaluation harness sending anonymized metrics through an approved path or just run entirely in your environment and we can ingest results via your secure upload.

[17:41] [17:41] (40-minute mark)

[17:50] Mateo: Let's talk about degraded quality detection — we need an early warning if quantization causes hallucination on certain doc types.

[17:56] Eleni: We integrate lightweight evaluation in the request path: a set of canary prompts that run periodically and compare embeddings + answer similarity. Drift triggers alerts. You can also configure prompt-level quality thresholds.

[18:18] Ava: For rollouts we prefer gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% if everything looks good.

[18:26] Jordan: That aligns with our canary tooling. We'll add a step in the rollout to re-run the canary prompt set after each promotion.

[18:40] Samir: About cost: can you ballpark infra delta between 8-bit and 4-bit for our size?

[18:47] Eleni: On storage alone 4-bit halves NVMe footprint vs 8-bit. Compute cost for dequant is small relative to attention ops, so net you see ~30-50% reduction in per-token billing equivalent in a hosted-like meter; on self-host it's roughly proportional to NVMe and GPU memory saved.

[19:08] [19:08] (closing planning section)

[19:15] Jordan: Okay let's recap and next steps.

[19:18] (recap bullet list from Jordan)
- Share perf harness and bench scripts (Jordan)
- Provide compliance packet and architecture diagrams (Jordan)
- Lynx to run benches and return CSVs for 4k/32k/128k baseline + bucketing tests (Lynx)
- Set up a Private trial tenant in their VPC with canary routing (Ops follow-up)

[19:45] Ava: Sounds good. Timeline: we'd like benches by Jan 10, then a pilot week Jan 17. Security review is on Jan 5.

[19:57] Jordan: We'll slot security packet earlier this week.

[20:05] Mateo: Quick note — when you send the harness, include recommended kernel builds and OS tunings.

[20:11] Eleni: Will do, and we'll include fio presets and scheduler tips.

[20:22] (some wrap-up chatter, social)

[20:45] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and links. End call.
